Sub-rules with implicit defaults

Rules that have no explicit annotation default to their grammar-shape envelope (see Parse Content Variants). The default is documented at the rule level in grammars/systemverilog.ebnf comments where the default is non-obvious.

Unannotated-on-purpose rules

Some rules will remain un-annotated by design — typically utility / helper rules whose envelope shape is the most useful representation, or rules whose typed shape would be redundant with their parent rule’s shape.

RuleReason
(none yet)(none yet)

Each row added here will cite the slice that decided the rule should remain un-annotated.

How to read the annotation column

The annotation column shows the EBNF -> ... clause from grammars/systemverilog.ebnf. The reference grammar for the annotation language is:

  • $N — positional reference to the Nth body element (1-indexed).
  • $N.field — member access on a typed sub-rule shape.
  • {field: value, ...} — typed object literal.
  • [v1, v2, ...] — array literal.
  • [$N**] — flatten-spread an array-shaped reference.
  • true / false / null — boolean / null scalars.
  • @transform — typed numeric value via str::parse::<TYPE>-style transform.
  • "text" — string literal.

See docs/contracts/PGEN_RETURN_ANNOTATION_PARSER_INTEGRATION_CONTRACT.md for the full annotation-language grammar.

The dist Constraint Operator

Parser release 1.0.179 (SV-CORPUS-GRAD.3.18, ledger SV-0049). Schema 19 → 20.

IEEE 1800-2017 A.2.10 defines the distribution operand as:

expression_or_dist ::= expression [ dist { dist_list } ]
dist_list          ::= dist_item { , dist_item }
dist_item          ::= value_range [ dist_weight ]
dist_weight        ::= := expression | :/ expression

⛔ The { } on the first line are literal SystemVerilog braces; the { } on the second line are BNF repetition. Two lines apart, same characters, opposite meanings. Before 1.0.179 the grammar read the first pair as repetition too, and the consequences were not limited to a rejection.

you writebefore 1.0.179from 1.0.179
x dist {100 := 1, 200 := 2}rejected at the :=parses
x dist { [100:102] :/ 1, 200 := 2}rejected at the [parses
soft x dist {5, 8};parses — but as one item whose value is the concatenation {5, 8}parses as the two items the LRM defines
x dist 100 := 1; (no braces)accepted — no such production existscorrectly rejected

The third row is the one to read twice. It parsed, so no pass/fail check anywhere reported it; the only visible symptom was in the emitted tree, where the dist item’s value carried "kind": "concat" instead of the individual values.

Migration

For any input that already parsed, the dist slot grew from two elements to four:

// before 1.0.179 — `soft x dist {5, 8};`
"dist": [ ["…","dist"], [ [ /* ONE item, value = concat of 5 and 8 */ ] ] ]

// from 1.0.179
"dist": [ ["…","dist"], {"kind":"lbrace"}, [ /* item 5 */, /* item 8 */ ], {"kind":"rbrace"} ]
  • A consumer that indexed dist[1] to reach the list must now read dist[2].
  • A consumer that read a single item whose value was a concatenation must now read the individual dist_items.

The pre-1.0.179 shape was a bug, not a stable schema — it could not represent a weighted distribution at all.

Bound worth knowing

dist_weight is modelled as the two tokens : = (and : /) rather than a fused := / :/, so interior white space — x dist {100 : = 1} — is currently tolerated where the LRM’s operator spelling arguably forbids it. That is a strictness question in the same family as the time_literal white-space item, tracked separately in docs/tasks/SV-CORPUS-GRAD.md; it is not introduced by this release and no corpus file depends on it.

The Config use Clause and Parameter Overrides

Parser release 1.0.180 (SV-CORPUS-GRAD.3.19, ledger SV-0050). Schema stays 20.

A config block selects which cell binds to which instance, and it can override parameters while doing so. Before 1.0.180 the parameter-override spelling that IEEE 1800’s own examples use did not parse at all:

config cfg;
  design rtlLib.top;
  instance top     use #(.WIDTH(32));      // rejected before 1.0.180
  instance top.a1  use #(.W(top.WIDTH));   // rejected before 1.0.180
  instance top.a1  use #();                // rejected before 1.0.180
endconfig

Why it was missing — the standard disagrees with itself

This is worth spelling out, because it is not the failure mode behind the other recent grammar fixes in this book. Those (SV-0044 cycle-delay ranges, SV-0049 the dist operator) were cases where the LRM wrote a literal delimiter and PGEN’s grammar read it as BNF metasyntax. Here PGEN’s transcription was right, and the standard is internally inconsistent:

  • Annex A / Syntax 33-4 defines use_clause with three alternatives and no # anywhere: use [lib.]cell [:config], use .P(1), …, use [lib.]cell .P(1), ….
  • Clause 33.4.3 then writes every one of its parameter-override examples as use #( … ) — seven times, and identically in both IEEE 1800-2017 and IEEE 1800-2023.

PGEN follows the union of the two, on three grounds that are internal to the standard rather than a matter of taste. Annex A’s preamble subordinates itself — “The normative text description contained within the clauses and annexes of this standard provide additional details on the syntax”. The BNF-only reading would make clause 33.4.3’s explicit “Configurations may not use positional parameter notation to override parameters” meaningless, since positional notation cannot even be written under the brace-less alternatives. And every parameter-override use clause in PGEN’s vendored external corpus — all 12 of them — uses the #( … ) spelling.

What still rejects, on purpose

instance top.a1 use #(32);            // REJECTED — positional override
instance top.a1 use #(32, .W(8));     // REJECTED — mixed positional

Clause 33.4.3 forbids positional parameter notation in a configuration, so the #( … ) list accepts named_parameter_assignment only. This is why the grammar does not reuse parameter_value_assignment — that rule is exactly # ( [ list_of_parameter_assignments ] ), and list_of_parameter_assignments admits ordered assignments. An ordinary module instantiation is unaffected and still accepts both notations:

adder #(8, 16)  a1();   // fine — ordinary instantiation, positional allowed
adder #(.W(8))  a2();   // fine

What a consumer sees

The use clause is carried as a raw token sequence inside its config_rule_statement, whose kind discriminator (inst_use / cell_use / inst_liblist / cell_liblist / default_liblist) tells you which shape to expect:

{"kind": "inst_use",
 "clause": {"name": {"head": {"body": "top"}, "scope_chain": []}},
 "body": [[[], "use"],
          {"kind": "hash"}, {"kind": "lparen"},
          [{"name": {"body": "WIDTH"}, "value": {"…": "32"}}, []],
          {"kind": "rparen"}, []]}

The {"kind": "hash"} / {"kind": "lparen"} / {"kind": "rparen"} markers are how you tell the braced form from the Annex-A brace-less one (use .WIDTH(32)), which carries the named assignments with no surrounding punctuation nodes.

Schema is unchanged at 20. This construct was 100 % unparseable before 1.0.180, so no shape a consumer had ever seen could move — verified by dumping the AST of every already-parsing form of the clause on both parsers and confirming all ten are byte-identical.

Which profiles accept the overrides

Parser release 1.0.181 (SV-CORPUS-GRAD.3.20, ledger SV-0051). Schema stays 20.

Parameter override in a config use clause is SystemVerilog-only. IEEE 1364-2005 declares exactly one use_clause alternative — use [library_identifier.]cell_identifier[:config] (Annex A A.1.5, restated in 13.3) — with no parameter override in any spelling, and the string use #( occurs nowhere in the 2005 text. Since 1.0.181 the parser matches that:

spellingsv_2017 / sv_2023verilog_2005
use adder; · use rtlLib.adder; · use rtlLib.adder:config;acceptaccept
use .W(8); · use .W(8), .D(16);acceptreject
use adder .W(8); · use rtlLib.adder .W(8);acceptreject
use #(.W(8)); · use #();acceptreject
use #(32); (positional — 33.4.3 forbids it)rejectreject

⛔ This restricts the config use clause only. An ordinary module instantiation’s parameter value assignment — adder #(8, 16) a1();, adder #(.W(8)) a2(); — is legal Verilog-2001/2005 and still accepts under every profile. The two surfaces look alike and are governed by different productions.

Mechanically, the four override alternatives live in a @profiles: ["sv_2017", "sv_2023"] sibling rule, use_clause_param_override_sv_only, referenced as use_clause’s first alternative. @profiles is a rule-level directive, so gating a subset of a rule’s alternatives always takes this shape; the house pattern is always_keyword / always_keyword_sv_only.

No consumer-visible shape change. Under sv_2017/sv_2023 the AST is byte-identical across the split — a bare rule-reference alternative carrying no return annotation adds no wrapper node — so existing inst_use / cell_use readers are unaffected. Under verilog_2005 the affected spellings no longer parse at all, so there is no shape to read. If a tool was relying on the old behaviour, it was requesting verilog_2005 while parsing SystemVerilog; request sv_2017 or sv_2023 instead.

Directives Inside Module and Class Bodies

Parser release 1.0.178 (SV-CORPUS-GRAD.3.14b, ledger SV-0048). Schema stays 19.

Before 1.0.178 a compiler directive was tolerated only at file top level. The rule compiler_directive was an alternative of source_text_item and of nothing else, so the identical text one line lower rejected:

`timescale 1ns / 1ps        // parsed
module m;
endmodule

module m;
  `timescale 1ns / 1ps      // REJECTED before 1.0.178
endmodule

A legally-placed directive now parses at module-body and class-body item positions, and appears in the item array as an ordinary typed item:

module m;
  `timescale 1ns / 1ps
  wire w;
endmodule

"items": [
  { "kind": "compiler_directive", "body": "`timescale 1ns / 1ps" },
  { "kind": "module_or_generate", "body": { "...": "the wire declaration" } }
]

The class-body form is identical in shape:

class c;
  `undef EVIL_MACRO
  int x;
endclass

"items": [
  { "kind": "compiler_directive", "body": "`undef EVIL_MACRO" },
  { "kind": "sv_2017", "body": { "...": "the int property" } }
]

⚠️ Consumer impact. non_port_module_item and class_item can now yield the kind compiler_directive, which previously appeared only under source_text. A consumer that matches those item kinds exhaustively must add the arm. The node itself is byte-identical to the top-level one — same kind, same string body — so no schema change is involved; only the container is new. ⚠️ The string bodies shown above are the 1.0.178–1.0.216 shape; since 1.0.217 (schema 29) the body is the typed node described in Typed Compiler Directives, at both containers alike.

Typed Compiler Directives (schema 29)

Parser release 1.0.217 (SV-CORPUS-GRAD.3.39, ledger SV-0090). Schema 28 → 29.

Through 1.0.216 every tolerated directive — at file top level and at the in-scope item positions — arrived as one opaque string: {"kind": "compiler_directive", "body": "timescale 1ns / 1ps“}. That carried two defects the corpus measured. A consumer received a line it had to re-lex itself, and the parser accepted any arguments at all: `` timescale frump , unconnected_drive pull2 ``, `` line 1 “f” 3 and a bare pragma `` all parsed (verilator t_timescale_parse_bad.v/t_unconnected_bad.v, sv-tests 22.12–line-illegal-.sv, sv2v test/error/line_.sv— 26 corpus files on thesv_2017` lane, every one a form the clause’s syntax box refuses).

IEEE 1800-2017 clause 22 gives thirteen directives a syntax box — each captioned “not in Annex A”, which is why no Annex-A-driven slice transcribed them — and 1.0.217 transcribes each box as a production. The body is now a typed node whose kind is the directive’s name:

`timescale 1 ns / 1 ps
`default_nettype none
`line 3 "orig.v" 2
`pragma protect encoding = (enctype = "BASE64", bytes = 128)
`begin_keywords "1364-2005"
`include "x.svh"

[
  { "kind": "compiler_directive", "body": { "kind": "timescale",
      "unit":      { "value": "1", "unit": { "kind": "ns" } },
      "precision": { "value": "1", "unit": { "kind": "ps" } } } },
  { "kind": "compiler_directive", "body": { "kind": "default_nettype", "value": { "kind": "none" } } },
  { "kind": "compiler_directive", "body": { "kind": "line", "number": "3",
      "filename": { "kind": "double_quoted", "body": "\"orig.v\"" }, "level": "2" } },
  { "kind": "compiler_directive", "body": { "kind": "pragma", "name": "protect", "expressions": [
      { "kind": "assignment", "keyword": "encoding", "value": { "kind": "group", "items": [
          { "kind": "assignment", "keyword": "enctype",
            "value": { "kind": "string", "body": { "kind": "double_quoted", "body": "\"BASE64\"" } } },
          { "kind": "assignment", "keyword": "bytes",
            "value": { "kind": "number", "body": { "kind": "integral", "body": "128" } } } ] } } ] } },
  { "kind": "compiler_directive", "body": { "kind": "begin_keywords",
      "version": { "kind": "double_quoted", "body": "\"1364-2005\"" } } },
  { "kind": "compiler_directive", "body": { "kind": "opaque", "text": "`include \"x.svh\"" } }
]
body.kindfieldsclause
resetall, celldefine, endcelldefine, nounconnected_drive, end_keywords, undefineall—§22.3, §22.10, §22.9, §22.14, §22.5.3
undefname (identifier node)§22.5.2
timescaleunit, precision ({value, unit: {kind}})§22.7
default_nettypevalue ({kind}, eleven values)§22.8
unconnected_drivevalue ({kind: "pull0" | "pull1"})§22.9
pragmaname, expressions (list; keyword / assignment / value; values group / number / string / identifier)§22.11
linenumber, filename (string node), level§22.12
begin_keywordsversion (string node)§22.14
opaquetext (the whole line, the 1.0.216 string)— the residue

Migration. body was a string; it is an object. Switch on body.kind. The residue — `include, `define, `ifdef / `else / `elsif / `endif / `ifndef, a text-macro use, a vendor directive such as `default_decay_time — keeps the string under body.text with body.kind == "opaque", and is still tolerated only at file top level (the .3.14b in-scope whitelist has no opaque branch). Files whose directives all had legal arguments change shape and nothing else; the accept set narrows exactly on the illegal forms (the pins stimuli/sv/adjudication_repros/invalid_directive_*.sv, and the corpus rows named in docs/tasks/artifacts/sv_corpus_grad/directive_census/census.md).

Three readings a consumer should know. (1) A newline between directive arguments is §5.3 white space — no box states a line rule, so `timescale 1ns ⏎ / 1ps parses (it did not on 1.0.216, whose opaque token ended at the newline); only `line is bound to its line, as §22.12 says (“only white space may appear on the same line … comments are not allowed”), and a bare-name `pragma is bounded to its line so it cannot swallow the next item’s first identifier. (2) The magnitude of a `timescale argument is syntax (1, 10, 100 — §22.7’s only definition of it), where Annex A’s own timeunit 2ps; stays derivable; the precision-ordering rule is a value rule and is not judged. (3) `begin_keywords admits exactly the edition’s list: "1800-2023" parses under sv_2023 and rejects under sv_2017 and verilog_2005; "1800-2017" rejects under verilog_2005.

Which directives are tolerated — and which are still rejected

The set is a whitelist derived from IEEE 1800-2017 clause 22 and IEEE 1364-2005 clause 19 read in full, not blanket tolerance of any backtick line. The two standards agree name for name; only `undefineall is SystemVerilog-only.

tolerated in-scopeclausewhy
`celldefine `endcelldefine§22.10 / §19.1“may appear anywhere in the source description”
`undef§22.5.2 / §19.3.2no placement restriction stated
`undefineall§22.5.3 (SV only)“may appear anywhere in the source description”
`timescale§22.7 / §19.8no placement restriction stated
`pragma§22.11 / §19.10no placement restriction stated
`line§22.12 / §19.7“can be specified anywhere within the … source description”

Everything else still rejects inside a design element, deliberately, and that half is as much part of the contract as the acceptances:

still rejected in-scopeclausewhy
`resetall§22.3 / §19.6“It shall be illegal … within a design element”
`default_nettype§22.8 / §19.2“can be used only outside design elements”
`unconnected_drive `nounconnected_drive§22.9 / §19.9“shall be specified outside the design element declarations”
`begin_keywords `end_keywords§22.14 / §19.11“can only be specified outside a design element”
`include `define `ifdef `ifndef `else `elsif `endif§22.4–§22.6 / §19.3–§19.5these hide or rewrite the text that follows, so the file is a preprocessing dependency rather than complete parser input
`__FILE__ `__LINE__ and any user macro§22.13these are predefined/user text macros, not directives — see below
 
module m;
  `default_nettype none     // still REJECTED — LRM permits it only outside design elements
endmodule

module m;
  `MY_MACRO(x)              // still REJECTED — an unexpanded macro use, not a directive
endmodule

⭐ Why the macro case matters. `MY_MACRO(x) at an item position expands to real module items. A blanket “tolerate any backtick line” rule would swallow the line, silently drop everything the macro expands to, and report a pass for a file the parser never actually understood. Rejecting it keeps an unexpanded file honestly distinguishable from a complete one. Directive names are matched with a trailing word boundary, so `timescale_like_macro and `undef_not_a_directive are macros, not directives.

Bounds worth knowing

  • Tolerance is at item positions — between items, never between two tokens of one statement. always @(posedge clk) timescale …` does not parse.
  • Hosts are module bodies and class bodies. Generate, interface, program, package and checker bodies still reject a legally-placed directive (docs/tasks/SV-CORPUS-GRAD.md .3.14d).
  • `pragma is tolerated as a line; its structured §22.11 content is not parsed and its effect is not modelled. A `pragma protect encrypted envelope (§34) still rejects, correctly — it stops at the base64 payload, not at the directive.
  • Top-level behaviour is unchanged: directives above/below a design element parsed before and parse identically now.

Typed Function and Task Bodies (schema 30)

Parser release 1.0.218 (SV-CORPUS-GRAD.3.44, ledger SV-0091). Schema 29 → 30.

IEEE 1800-2017 A.2.6 / A.2.7 give a function or task body exactly two forms, each with an optional out-of-block prefix:

function_body_declaration ::=
    function_data_type_or_implicit [ interface_identifier . | class_scope ] function_identifier ;
        { tf_item_declaration } { function_statement_or_null } endfunction [ : function_identifier ]
  | function_data_type_or_implicit [ interface_identifier . | class_scope ] function_identifier ( [ tf_port_list ] ) ;
        { block_item_declaration } { function_statement_or_null } endfunction [ : function_identifier ]
task_body_declaration ::= (the same two forms, without the return type)

The grammar spells that as four alternatives — the prefix × the port list — and through 1.0.217 only the first (type f; … endfunction, its ports declared INSIDE the body) carried a return template. The other three arrived as the raw Sequence envelope: a positional array the consumer had to index by hand, with the port list at [3] on a ported function and at [4] on an out-of-block ported one. The corpus census on the 1.0.217 probe (AST-FIELD-CENSUS: with the new --select-keys lifetime,body selector + TF-BODY-CLASSIFY:) read 2 211 of the 3 411 function / task bodies the parser wrote on sv_2017 as that raw envelope — 1 646 ported functions, 513 ported tasks, 30 out-of-block functions, 22 out-of-block tasks — in 1 060 of the 1 958 accepting files that declare a function or task at all. The ported form is the most common function in any corpus, and the typed AST could not read it.

Since 1.0.218 every alternative is typed, mirroring alternative 1’s field set:

function int f;  input int a;  return a;  endfunction                 // alt 1 (unchanged)
function int f(int a);  return a;  endfunction : f                   // alt 2 — ports present
function void I.h;  input int a;  endfunction                        // alt 3 — scope present
function int C::g(int a, int b = 2);  return a * b;  endfunction    // alt 4 — scope and ports present

{"return_type": {"kind": "data_type", "body": {…}}, "name": {"body": "f"}, "items": [{"kind": "tf_port", "body": {…}}], "statements": […], "end_label": []}
{"return_type": {…}, "name": {"body": "f"}, "ports": [{…}], "items": [], "statements": […], "end_label": [{"kind": "colon"}, {"body": "f"}]}
{"return_type": {…}, "scope": [{"body": "I"}, {"kind": "dot"}], "name": {"body": "h"}, "items": [{"kind": "tf_port", "body": {…}}], "statements": [], "end_label": []}
{"return_type": {…}, "scope": {"body": {"head": {"body": "C"}, "params": [], "scope_chain": []}}, "name": {"body": "g"}, "ports": [{…}, {…}], "items": [], "statements": […], "end_label": []}

How a consumer tells the forms apart. There is no kind: the discriminator is key PRESENCE, which is the standard’s own distinction. ports is present exactly on the ported alternatives (2 and 4) — it is the typed tf_port_list array, [] for f() — and scope exactly on the out-of-block ones (3 and 4), carrying the out_of_block_tf_scope node: the pair [<interface_identifier>, {kind: "dot"}] for an interface method (§25.7) or the class_scope node for a class method (§8.24). The two forms also differ in items, faithfully: a NON-ported body’s items are tf_item_declaration nodes, {kind: "block_item" | "tf_port", body}, because that is where its ports live; a ported body’s items are bare block_item_declaration nodes, because A.2.6’s second production admits no port declaration there. A consumer that switched on the array length before now reads "ports" in body and "scope" in body.

Migration. A consumer of schema 29 that indexed the raw envelope — body[0] for the return type, body[3] / body[4] for the port list, body[6] / body[7] / body[8] for the items — reads the named fields instead; the elements are the same typed nodes in the same order, with the lparen / rparen / semi / endfunction tokens dropped as they are on alternative 1. Alternative 1 itself is byte-identical (measured: the two in-block pins and every all-typed corpus file). A REPLACEMENT of a raw envelope by a typed node is the SV-0014…SV-0020 corruption-fix precedent, hence the bump.

Measured over the corpus. The corpus AST identity sweep (the 1.0.217 probe vs this release, TOOLBOX §1.5e) reads AST-IDENTITY-SWEEP: profile=sv_2017 files=16336 both_accepted=9756 identical=8696 ast_moved=1060 verdict_moved=0 both_nonaccepting=6580 and AST-IDENTITY-SWEEP: profile=sv_2023 files=16336 both_accepted=9780 identical=8716 ast_moved=1064 verdict_moved=0 both_nonaccepting=6556, and over the verilog_2005 lane AST-IDENTITY-SWEEP: profile=verilog_2005 files=2606 both_accepted=2310 identical=2270 ast_moved=40 verdict_moved=0 both_nonaccepting=296 — two-sided against the census’s prediction (sv_2017: predicted 1060, moved 1060, predicted-but-identical 0, moved-but-not-predicted 0; sv_2023: predicted 1064, moved 1064, predicted-but-identical 0, moved-but-not-predicted 0; verilog_2005: predicted 40, moved 40, predicted-but-identical 0, moved-but-not-predicted 0). No verdict moves on any lane (a return template changes what the parser emits, never what it accepts): sv_2017 transitions: NONE (pass 9756 / fail 6580 of 16336 rows, 0 timeouts); sv_2023 transitions: NONE (pass 9780 / fail 6556 of 16336 rows, 0 timeouts); verilog_2005 transitions: NONE (pass 2310 / fail 296 of 2606 rows, 0 timeouts). Eight pins — one per alternative of each rule, the two in-block ones as the controls that cannot move (control_tf_body_*.sv, arms tf_port / !tf_port pinning WHERE the ports live) — and six AST-shape contract samples, one per newly typed alternative, parsed AS the body rule.

Profiles. The ported alternatives are legal IEEE 1364-2005 too (A.2.6 function_port_list, A.2.7 task_port_list), so the verilog_2005 profile’s typed AST moves on the same forms; the out-of-block alternatives are SV-only (interfaces and classes) and reject there as before.

Typed Partial Alternatives (schema 31)

Schema 32 addendum (1.0.220, SV-CORPUS-GRAD.3.46). The one block_data body this section left without a kind — alternative 1, the block-scoped integer VECTOR reg [7:0] v; / logic [3:0] t;, typed by SV-Slice-96 as {base, signing, dims} — now carries data_type’s own {kind: "integer_vector", base, signing, dims}. A REPLACEMENT: a reader that recognised the vector form by the ABSENCE of kind reads kind == "integer_vector"; every other alternative is byte-identical. Pre-registered by this section’s own census (712 nodes in 259 accepting files per SV lane, 130 in 73 on the 1364-2005 lane) and measured two-sided by the corpus AST identity sweep: every predicted file moved, no other accepted tree moved a byte, no verdict moved. From schema 32 every alternative a consumer can meet on the block_data body carries a kind or is a passed-through child — the body is discriminated by kind exactly as data_type is.

Parser release 1.0.219 (SV-CORPUS-GRAD.3.45, ledger SV-0092). Schema 30 → 31.

1.0.218 closed with the class measured: the partial-typing census (TOOLBOX §1.5g) read 38 rules typed on some alternatives and not others, 19 of the untyped alternatives raw envelopes, in eight rules. A raw envelope is the positional Sequence array a consumer indexes by hand; every one of the nineteen was a consumer-facing shape. The corpus census on the 1.0.218 probe (RAW-ENVELOPE-CENSUS:, TOOLBOX §1.5h, every lane row) read 2 319 of them in 1 088 accepting files on sv_2017 (1 779 / 819 on sv_2023, 217 / 120 on the 1364-2005 lane):

Migration. A consumer that indexed a raw envelope reads the named fields; the elements are the same typed nodes in the same order, with the punctuation and keyword tokens dropped. Concretely: pattern[2] / pattern[4] and each [comma, key, colon, expr] iteration → keys[i] / values[i]; body[0] / body[1] of a block integer atom → base / signing; the case envelope’s [3] expression and [6] / [7] items → expr, items.first, items.rest; the clocking envelope’s [2] / [3] / [6] → name / event / end_label; the event envelope’s [2] → body; the comma-separated delay list → the LRM position names; the property default arm’s [2] → body.

The nettype alias form was shadowed, not raw. IEEE 1800-2017 §6.6.7 gives a nettype declaration a second form, another name for an existing nettype: nettype wTsum nettypeid2;. On the LRM’s own example both alternatives of net_type_declaration_sv_2017 succeed — a declared nettype is a type_name fact, so the data-type form reads wTsum as a known_unscoped_data_type — and the longest-match tie went to declaration order: the alias alternative NEVER won, on either SV profile (the fully typed sv_2023 twin included), and the AST called the base nettype a data type. Since 1.0.219 the data-type alternative REFUSES an alias head by negative lookahead — since 1.0.239 (SV-CORPUS-GRAD.27) !( nettype_alias_shape_ahead ): [ scope ] <declared nettype> <identifier> (the trailing ; left the lookahead in .3.46, so a declared nettype base is refused with or without a with clause — pinned invalid_nettype_alias_with_resolution_function.sv), OR the exact alias form <unresolved bare name> <identifier> ; under an open wildcard import (!( checked_type_identifier ) wildcard_escape_nettype_identifier declaration_identifier semi), which the .27 type escape in data_type would otherwise read as a data type and win the longest-match tie — the first 1.0.239 candidate did, and the pins pre-screen read ast_moved=2 before any lane ran; a declared type is not the shape, so nettype T wT; over a typedef keeps the data-type reading — so the alias alternative wins those declarations while the order stays as shipped; and the alias base net_type_identifier, a bare declaration_identifier through 1.0.218 (one ungated twin per edition), is checked_nettype_identifier | wildcard_escape_nettype_identifier — a declared nettype, or an undeclared name under a wildcard import, exactly how net_declaration reads a net of a user-defined nettype (SV-PARSE-STRICT.2; SV-0037 routed the same ungated names in net_port_type) — the three ungated twins deleted. Two spellings were refuted first: reordering the ungated alternative read nettype T wT; (T a struct typedef, ispras 06.07.02_01.sv) as an alias — the two-sided corpus sweep caught it as the one moved-but-not-predicted file — and reordering the gated one broke the certificate’s own nettype prelude: the generator renders an unplanned declaration with the first of two equally cheap alternatives, so checked_nettype_identifier’s witness prelude became nettype \foo \foo;, an alias with an undeclared base, and the union certificate read UNKNOWN=2 where 1.0.218 had 0. Order is a generation contract as much as a parsing one. The alias alternative now wins exactly the alias declarations; the corpus carries two per SV lane (verilator t_nettype.v, ispras 06.06.07_01.sv), pre-registered by the census’s alias_shadowed note and moved by the release. ⚠️ One narrowing: nettype undeclared_t x; with no wildcard import in scope was accepted through 1.0.218 down the ungated alias alternative and is LRM-illegal (§6.6.7: the base must be an existing nettype); it now rejects on both SV profiles — the census read 0 accepting corpus files down that alternative, and invalid_nettype_alias_undeclared_base.sv pins it.

Two non-LRM alternatives removed. list_of_path_delay_expressions had carried seven alternatives since the grammar’s first promotion where IEEE 1364-2005, 1800-2017 and 1800-2023 all give five: a second six-value spelling that matched the same text as the LRM’s six-value form and lost the longest-match tie to it on every input (Protocol D: six values selected branch 4/7), and a twelve-value spelling whose middle four positions were the regex terminal /tx_path_delay_expression\b/ — the production NAME extracted as literal source text, matched by no file in the corpus. Neither could produce a tree; both are gone, with their orphaned keyword terminal — with the three ungated nettype identifier twins, 1641 → 1637 rules.

Measured over the corpus. The corpus AST identity sweep (the 1.0.218 probe vs this release, every lane row, TOOLBOX §1.5e) and the lanes’ verdicts are recorded in the integration contract’s 1.0.219 note and the census artifact docs/tasks/artifacts/sv_corpus_grad/partial_typing_residue/census.md; the partial-typing census reads RAW_ENVELOPE=0 on the released grammar (31 partial rules remain, all of them passthrough alternatives typed one level down by design).

The Opt-In Tolerance Profile (sv_2023_tolerant, since 1.0.249)

sv_2017, sv_2023 and verilog_2005 are strict: text the standard does not derive is rejected. Real verification code also contains a few spellings the commercial simulators accept and the standard does not. By director decision (2026-10-02) the parser carries ONE opt-in profile for them: sv_2023_tolerant is sv_2023 plus a closed list of five spellings (four since 1.0.249, the fifth since 1.0.250), and nothing else. Nothing selects it unless the caller names it; there is no alias and no convenience entry point — use the generic named entry (parse_grammar_profile_named("systemverilog", "sv_2023_tolerant", …)) or --profile sv_2023_tolerant.

What it accepts that sv_2023 does not

spellingexamplethe standard’s own formwhat the standard says
foreach with bracket pairs before the loop-variable bracketforeach (a[i][j])foreach (a[i, j])§12.7.3: the argument is “an identifier that designates any type of array followed by a comma-separated list of loop variables enclosed in square brackets”
solve … before …; directly inside the braces of a foreach constraintforeach (x[i]) { solve y before x[i]; }the solve at constraint-block levelA.1.10: solve is a constraint BLOCK item; a foreach holds constraint expressions
a dotted name as a cross itemcross cp_a, cfg.vif.sig;declare a coverpoint for it, cross the coverpoint§19.6: “Expressions cannot be used directly in a cross; a coverage point must be explicitly defined first”
a lifetime in a CLASS method prototypepure virtual task automatic t();, extern function automatic T f();the prototype without the lifetimeA.2.6 / A.2.7 prototypes have no lifetime; §8.6 makes every class method automatic already
a hierarchical NAME of three or more parts inside binsof(…) (since 1.0.250)binsof(cfg.vif.sig) intersect {1}declare a coverpoint for the variable, name the coverpoint in the binsof§19.6.1: binsof “yields the bins of its expression, which can be either a coverage point … or a coverage point bin”; Syntax 19-4 derives a variable name, or a coverpoint name with an optional bin name, and nothing longer

What a consumer sees

Every tolerated spelling arrives under a kind no standard spelling produces, so a consumer can accept, flag or refuse it explicitly. The standard spellings keep their existing kinds and shapes under this profile.

rulenew kind (tolerant profile only)shape
loop_statement_sv_only"foreach_tolerated_select"{head, body} — head is {array, selects, loop_vars}: selects lists the expressions of the leading bracket pairs, in order; loop_vars is the LAST bracket pair, the standard loop_variables list
constraint_expression"foreach_tolerated_select"{head, body} — as above, body a standard constraint_set
constraint_expression"foreach_tolerated_solve"{array, loop_vars, body} — the standard foreach fields; body is {items}, each item a standard constraint_block_item ("solve_before" or "expression")
constraint_expression"foreach_tolerated_select_solve"{head, body} — both tolerances at once
cross_item"tolerated_hierarchical"{body} — body is {path}, a standard hierarchical_identifier
bins_expression (since 1.0.250)"tolerated_hierarchical"{body} — body is {path}, a standard hierarchical_identifier: the SAME shape the tolerated cross item carries, so the name a cross declares and the name its binsof selects are one node kind
class_method"pure_virtual_tolerated_lifetime"{qualifiers, prototype} — prototype is {kind, dynamic_override, lifetime, name, ports} with kind "task" or "function" (plus return_type for a function)
class_method"extern_tolerated_lifetime"{qualifiers, prototype} — the same prototype object

⚠️ A TWO-part name inside binsof keeps its standard reading under every profile. binsof(a.b) is, by syntax, cover_point_identifier . bin_identifier — {kind: "cover_point", name, bin} — whether a.b is a coverpoint’s bin or a variable reached through a handle; the parser cannot tell them apart and does not try. The tolerated kind begins at the THIRD name part (binsof(a.b.c)), which no standard production derives.

⚠️ The parser does not decide what foreach (a[i][j]) MEANS. A simulator may read i as a select by an enclosing variable (OpenTitan’s use) or as a second loop variable (Verilator’s and Surelog’s tests). The AST keeps the leading pairs apart as selects and leaves the reading to the consumer’s elaboration.

What it still rejects, on purpose

The list is closed and exact. Still rejected under sv_2023_tolerant: a solve under an if nested inside the foreach; a lifetime in a modport or interface-class prototype; an expression (y + 1) as a cross item; an EXPRESSION, a TRAILING SELECT or a CALL inside binsof(…) (binsof(cfg.vif.a + 1), binsof(cfg.vif.w[0]), binsof(cfg.vif.f()) — the tolerance is the hierarchical NAME and nothing else); and everything sv_2023 rejects for any other reason. Each of these boundaries is a reproducer pin.

Bounds worth knowing

  • The corpus lanes’ primary reading stays sv_2017; the tolerant profile has its own reading of the pipeline lane and its own census against sv_2023. It moves no published pass rate of the edition profiles.
  • The profile is held to its definition by a doctrine (SV-TOLERANT-PROFILE-SUPERSET: every rule live under sv_2023 is live under the tolerant profile; a tolerant-only rule is named tolerated_…) and by the pin runner’s superset sweep (every sv_2023 pin reads the same verdict under the tolerant profile).
  • A spelling joins the list only with a ruling: its LRM text read, its corpus count, a reproducer pair.
  • The recognized certificate (its universe: the rules live under sv_2017) does not count the tolerant rules. Under the tolerant profile’s own base, certificate coverage reads total=1564 proof=23 witness=1532 UNKNOWN=9 at seeds 0 / 7 / 42 (release 1.0.250): seven of the eleven tolerated_* rules are witnessed by generation. Four are not — the three solve-tolerance rules and tolerated_bins_expression_hierarchical — and for one measured reason: each begins with a lookahead, the witness planner renders the body’s MINIMAL expansion (one constraint expression and no solve; a one-part name), the lookahead does not hold on it, and the text parses through the standard alternative (parsed=true witnessed_target=false on the certificate’s debug probe). They are exercised on the generated parser by the reproducer pins and by the corpus instead; the planner gap is routed as ENGINE-UNIVERSAL-SERVICES.120. ⛔ Through 1.0.249 this paragraph gave another reason for the three solve rules (a generated solve … before naming variables a store gate had not seen); the probe shows no solve in any forced sample, and the sentence is corrected here.

Walking the AST

This chapter is a recommended walker pattern for downstream consumers traversing the SystemVerilog AST dump JSON.

The dual-shape walker

Because the annotation campaign types rules incrementally, the AST tree carries a mix of typed objects and recursive-envelope arrays. The walker dispatches on JSON value kind:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use serde_json::Value as JsonValue;

fn walk(node: &JsonValue) {
    match node {
        JsonValue::Object(obj) => {
            // Typed-shape node — dispatch on `type` / `kind` fields.
            let ty = obj.get("type").and_then(|v| v.as_str()).unwrap_or("");
            match ty {
                "module"      => walk_module(obj),
                "interface"   => walk_interface(obj),
                "class"       => walk_class(obj),
                // ... (other typed shapes; see per-rule chapters)
                _ => {
                    // Unknown typed shape — fall through to generic
                    // child walk. This keeps the walker robust to new
                    // typed shapes added in subsequent slices.
                    for (_key, value) in obj.iter() {
                        walk(value);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        JsonValue::Array(items) => {
            // Recursive-envelope shape — walk children.
            for item in items {
                walk(item);
            }
        }
        JsonValue::String(text) => {
            // Terminal text — no children. Use as identifier / literal
            // value if your traversal needs it.
        }
        JsonValue::Bool(_) | JsonValue::Number(_) | JsonValue::Null => {
            // Annotation-produced scalars (booleans for negation flags,
            // numbers for typed integer transforms, null for absent
            // optional fields). No children.
        }
    }
}
}

Why the unknown-typed-shape fallback matters

The walker pattern above includes a fallthrough that walks the children of any typed object the walker doesn’t know about:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
_ => {
    for (_key, value) in obj.iter() {
        walk(value);
    }
}
}

This is important because the annotation campaign adds new typed shapes over time. A walker that hard-fails on unknown type values will break on every parser-release that adds a new typed rule. A walker that walks children of unknown typed shapes degrades gracefully — it won’t extract structured info for shapes it doesn’t understand, but it’ll still find descendants.

Recommendation: only hard-fail on unknown shapes when you’re explicitly pinning to a specific AST-dump schema version (the constant you pin from the contract — see Schema-version-aware walking below) and your test corpus covers every type value in that schema.

Identifier extraction

For SystemVerilog identifiers (module names, signal names, etc.), look for the rule that produces the identifier and walk to its terminal text:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn extract_identifier(node: &JsonValue) -> Option<&str> {
    // Once `simple_identifier` carries a typed annotation, this
    // becomes obj.get("name").as_str() directly. Until then, walk
    // to the matched terminal text.
    match node {
        JsonValue::String(text) => Some(text.as_str()),
        JsonValue::Array(items) if items.len() == 1 => {
            extract_identifier(&items[0])
        }
        _ => None,
    }
}
}

The per-rule chapters (e.g. Top-Level Rules) document the path for each rule that produces an identifier in its envelope.

Avoiding deep recursion

SystemVerilog can produce very deep AST trees — a real-world module with N hierarchical instances + class hierarchies + always blocks easily reaches 200-500 levels of nesting. Stack-recursive walkers can blow the default Rust thread stack on large inputs.

Recommendations:

  1. Use an explicit stack-based walker (push children, pop work items in a loop) instead of recursive function calls. The walker becomes iterative; stack depth is irrelevant.
  2. Or use the stacker crate to grow the thread stack as needed. PGEN itself uses this approach internally for the parser; consumers can do the same for AST traversal.
  3. For pure AST drop (releasing all the JSON values once parsing is done), use a non-recursive drop — serde_json::Value’s default Drop is recursive and can blow the stack on deeply-nested values. PGEN’s test path uses run_with_regex_worker_stack (a 64MB-stack worker) to avoid this; downstream consumers should consider similar patterns.

Schema-version-aware walking

AstDumpPayload has no schema_version (or root) field — the real struct is dump_json/truncated/full_bytes/emitted_bytes. The AST-dump schema version is not discoverable at runtime from the payload; you pin it from docs/contracts/PGEN_SYSTEMVERILOG_PARSER_INTEGRATION_CONTRACT.md § “Contract Identity” as a constant in your consumer and re-validate that pin against the contract’s “Schema Versioning” table whenever you bump PGEN. The shape-contract manifest (rust/test_data/ast_shape_contract/systemverilog_v1.json) is the machine-checkable lock that fails CI if the parser drifts from the pinned schema.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// The AST-dump schema version you integrated against (from the contract):
const SV_AST_SCHEMA_VERSION: u32 = 3;

let payload = outcome.ast_dump.expect("Success carries an AstDumpPayload");
if payload.truncated {
    // dump_json holds the truncation diagnostic envelope, not the AST.
    return Err("systemverilog AST dump truncated".into());
}
let root: serde_json::Value = serde_json::from_str(&payload.dump_json)?;

// SV_AST_SCHEMA_VERSION selects which walker your code was built for.
// When you bump PGEN, diff the contract's Schema Versioning table; if the
// integer schema version moved, update the constant and the walker together.
match SV_AST_SCHEMA_VERSION {
    3 => walk_schema_v3(&root), // current: list_of_*_identifiers / *_list_of_arguments / parameter_port_list type_only / assignment_pattern named are clean factored record lists (was structured {first:{…},rest} / {first_name,first_value,rest} at schema 2)
    2 => walk_schema_v2(&root), // legacy: net_alias is {lvalues: […]}; the above rules still {first:{…},rest}
    1 => walk_schema_v1(&root), // legacy: net_alias was {first, second, rest}
    other => eprintln!("no walker compiled for systemverilog AST schema version {other}"),
}
}

See Schema Versioning for what triggers a schema bump and what stays stable within a single schema version.

Entry points by profile

ProfileEntry ruleDescription
sv_2017systemverilog_file (per LRM Annex A.1.1)IEEE 1800-2017 source file.
sv_2023systemverilog_file (per LRM Annex A.1.1, with 2023 deltas)IEEE 1800-2023 source file. Same entry rule symbol; the 2023 grammar differs in interior rules where the LRM was extended.

Both profiles share grammars/systemverilog.ebnf as the single source. The profile selection determines which top-level dispatcher rule is used at parse time.

systemverilog_file (typed since SV-Slice-1)

Per grammars/systemverilog.ebnf line 184:

systemverilog_file := trivia source_text trivia
                   -> {type: "systemverilog_file", source_text: $2}

The annotation produces a typed JSON object at the root of every sv_2017 / sv_2023 parse. For an input like "module m; endmodule\n":

{
  "type": "systemverilog_file",
  "source_text": [/* source_text envelope */]
}

The source_text field is a flat array of source_text_item shapes (since SV-Slice-2 — see source_text (flat array since SV-Slice-2) below). Consumers walking the SV AST should dispatch on obj["type"] == "systemverilog_file" at the root level.

source_text (flat array since SV-Slice-2)

Per grammars/systemverilog.ebnf line 2273:

source_text := source_text_item*
            -> [$1**]

The [$1**] flatten-spread idiom produces a clean flat array of source_text_item shapes. Pre-SV-Slice-2 this was the raw Quantified envelope of the iteration; consumers walking obj["source_text"] had to descend through a Quantified wrap. Post-fix the array is consumer-ready — iterate directly:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
for item in obj["source_text"].as_array().unwrap() {
    walk_source_text_item(item);
}
}

For module m; endmodule\n, source_text has length 1 (the single module_declaration source-text item). For a multi-construct file (multiple modules + interfaces + packages), it carries one item per top-level construct in source order.

The inner source_text_item shapes are still raw envelope (Or of description | local_parameter_declaration semi | parameter_declaration semi | package_import_declaration | bind_directive | ...). Per-branch typing of source_text_item is a follow-up slice (will assign each branch a kind: discriminator).

See rust/test_data/ast_shape_contract/systemverilog_v1.json for the calibrated regression-lock sample.

description (un-annotated)

description is the per-construct top-level alternative — module / interface / class / package / etc. Per LRM A.1.2:

description = module_declaration
            | udp_declaration
            | interface_declaration
            | program_declaration
            | package_declaration
            | (attribute_instance* package_item)
            | (attribute_instance* bind_directive)
            | config_declaration

Un-annotated description produces the matched-branch shape directly (no extra wrapping). When a slice annotates the per-branch dispatch, this rule will likely become:

description -> {type: "description", kind: "<branch>", body: $1}

(or similar) — actual annotation lands per-slice with the corresponding manifest update.

After the first slice

Once the first annotation slice lands, this chapter will document:

  • The -> ... annotation that landed on each top-level rule.
  • A worked example (input → JSON tree) for module m; endmodule\n.
  • The cumulative manifest entries.

For now, consult the Walking the AST walker pattern and use the recursive-envelope walk path for top-level rules.

How to follow per-slice changes

Each annotation slice gets a row in Schema Versioning and a Highlights section in docs/contracts/PGEN_SYSTEMVERILOG_PARSER_INTEGRATION_CONTRACT.md. A row in the Changelog Index ties the two together with a one-paragraph summary.

Worked Example: Minimal Module

A “what does the AST actually look like” walkthrough for the simplest possible SystemVerilog input.

Input

module m; endmodule

(Note the trailing newline — the parser typically requires it for EOF handling on the final construct.)

Pre-annotation (recursive envelope)

Until the annotation campaign types systemverilog_file and its descendants, the AST dump for the minimal module is the recursive-envelope shape — a JSON tree of arrays and strings reflecting the grammar’s sequence / quantified / alternation structure.

The exact shape is recorded in rust/test_data/ast_shape_contract/systemverilog_v1.json once the parser has been run for first calibration:

{
  "version": 1,
  "grammar": "systemverilog",
  "samples": [
    {
      "name": "minimal_module",
      "input": "module m; endmodule\n",
      "rule_under_test": "systemverilog_file",
      "current_content_kind": "<calibrated_after_first_run>",
      "expected_json_object_keys_present": [],
      ...
    }
  ]
}

The current_content_kind field is the regression-lock key — once calibrated, any drift in the AST dump shape will fail the cargo test AST-shape contract test, surfacing the change to the slice that introduced it.

Post-annotation (typed shape — landing per slice)

Once the first annotation slice lands and types systemverilog_file, this section will show:

// Hypothetical post-slice shape — actual annotation lands per-slice:
{
  "type": "systemverilog_file",
  "items": [
    {
      "type": "description",
      "kind": "module_declaration",
      "name": "m",
      "ports": [],
      "items": []
    }
  ]
}

(The actual shape lands when the slice is implemented and verified; this example is a placeholder showing the expected pattern.)

Walker code for this input

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use pgen::embedding_api::{
    parse_grammar_profile_ast_dump_named, AstDumpOptions, ParseStatus,
};

let outcome = parse_grammar_profile_ast_dump_named(
    "systemverilog",
    "sv_2017",
    "module m; endmodule\n",
    &AstDumpOptions { pretty: true, max_ast_bytes: None },
);

// AST-dump schema version you integrated against, pinned from the
// contract (NOT a field of AstDumpPayload):
const SV_AST_SCHEMA_VERSION: u32 = 3;

match outcome.status {
    ParseStatus::Success => {
        let ast_dump = outcome.ast_dump.expect("Success outcome carries AST dump");
        assert!(!ast_dump.truncated, "dump_json would hold the truncation envelope");
        let _ = SV_AST_SCHEMA_VERSION; // re-check vs the contract on PGEN bumps

        // AstDumpPayload exposes dump_json/truncated/full_bytes/emitted_bytes;
        // parse dump_json to get the typed root object.
        let root: serde_json::Value = serde_json::from_str(&ast_dump.dump_json)
            .expect("dump_json is valid JSON");
        assert_eq!(root["type"], "systemverilog_file");
        println!("AST root: {}", serde_json::to_string_pretty(&root).unwrap());
    }
    ParseStatus::Failure => {
        eprintln!("parse failed: {:?}", outcome.diagnostic);
    }
}
}

Why this example is the canonical first-test

The minimal module is the canonical first-test for SV parser integration because:

  • It exercises systemverilog_file → description → module_declaration — three layers of the top-level dispatch.
  • It has no statements, ports, or parameters — so the AST tree is shallow enough to reason about by hand.
  • It is in the integration contract manifest as minimal_module — drift here surfaces immediately.

If your downstream integration cannot parse this input successfully, the integration is broken upstream of any SV-specific concern. Start here when triaging.

Schema Versioning

This chapter explains how the SystemVerilog parser’s AST shape is versioned, what guarantees consumers can rely on, and how to pin to a known shape.

Two versioning axes

The systemverilog parser carries two version numbers:

  1. Parser release version — e.g. 1.0.0. Tracks the parser library’s release identity. Bumped on every functional change to the parser, including bug fixes, perf work, and grammar changes.
  2. Schema version — e.g. 1. Tracks the AST output shape. Bumped only when the output shape changes in a way consumers may need to adapt to.

A single parser release can carry the same schema version as the previous release (no shape change) or a bumped schema version (shape changed). The two version numbers move independently.

The contract document docs/contracts/PGEN_SYSTEMVERILOG_PARSER_INTEGRATION_CONTRACT.md is the authoritative source for both numbers per release.

What “shape change” means

Any of these triggers a schema version bump:

  • A new return annotation lands on a previously-unannotated rule.
  • An existing return annotation is restructured.
  • A grammar rule changes shape in a way that’s user-visible (new branch added, branch removed, sub-rule renamed in a way that affects shape).
  • The default fall-through behavior of unannotated rules changes.

These do NOT trigger a schema bump:

  • Pure performance optimizations that produce the same AST.
  • Internal codegen reorganization that doesn’t reach the output.
  • Parser-side bug fixes that produce the same shape consumers were already relying on.

The slice campaign for SV will produce many small schema bumps as rules are annotated one-by-one. Each slice gets its own contract-version row.

Byte-equivalence guarantee

For any input the parser accepts, the AST dump is byte-deterministic for a given parser-release version: object keys in canonical order, canonical number formatting, no embedded timestamps or hashes. Re-running the parse on the same input produces an identical JSON value.

This determinism is a hard guarantee of the schema. Any non-determinism is a bug — please report via docs/contracts/PGEN_PARSER_ISSUE_REPORTING_PROTOCOL.md.

It did not — a bare rule-reference alternative carrying no return annotation is AST-transparent, adding no wrapper node. Measured two independent ways: cmp-identical ASTs on 15/15 accepting repro cases under sv_2017, and the use_clause_hash_named_override shape lock’s observed content_kind unchanged (the lock is compared against a live parse on every gate run, so it is an oracle, not a note). ⭐ The lesson generalizes: “I restructured the grammar” is not by itself a schema bump, and “I only added a rule” is not by itself a non-bump — the AST is the arbiter, and it is cheap to ask. 27 (was 26)1.0.213SV-CORPUS-GRAD.3.41 (PGEN-SV-CORPUS-GRAD-0368, 2026-09-04), ledger SV-0086 — THE SET-MEMBERSHIP OPERATOR IS A CHAIN ELEMENT. inside_expression := expression_base inside { open_range_list } wrapped its LEFT operand and was reachable only at the top of expression, so a inside {…} & ~b REJECTED (the chain could not continue past the }) and b & a inside {…} derived as (b & a) inside {…} — a wrong tree on accepted text; IEEE 1800-2017 Table 11-2 (11.3.2) puts inside on the relational row, above ==, &, ^, |, &&, ||. 3 (unchanged)1.0.125SV-EXH-PROOF.3.3.4.b.1 (PGEN-SV-EXH-PROOF-0028, 2026-05-21). First LRM-extraction-defect fix. grammars/systemverilog.ebnf:1111’s conditional_statement was encoded with &kw_else_ae050f5b kw_else_ae050f5b conditional_else_branch (no | no-else alternative) → required else. Per IEEE 1800-2017 PDF page 1164 AND IEEE 1800-2023 PDF page 1201 (both identical): conditional_statement ::= [ unique_priority ] if ( cond_predicate ) statement_or_null { else if ( cond_predicate ) statement_or_null } [ else statement_or_null ]. Square brackets = OPTIONAL. Fix: helper rule conditional_else_clause := kw_else_ae050f5b conditional_else_branch -> $2; rewrote conditional_statement to … statement_or_null ( conditional_else_clause )? with else_body: $7 (was $9, now nullable). Removed dead mis-attached line 1116 (`

3 (unchanged)1.0.121SV-EXH-PROOF.3.3.3 (PGEN-SV-EXH-PROOF-0024, 2026-05-20). First deliberate ENGINE change in the SV-EXH-PROOF tree — parser-agnostic, benefits every grammar. Root cause (SEMTRACE-definitively-pinned after 3 prior hypotheses disproven): a Rust ?-bypasses-cleanup bug in the generator-emitted with_semantic_runtime_rule_transaction (rust/src/ast_pipeline/ast_based_generator.rs). The wrapper std::mem::take-s self.semantic_runtime_state (leaving Default==new() valid-but-EMPTY) and then performs ?-fallible calls; a ? early-return propagated out of the ENTIRE function, JUMPING OVER the trailing if result.is_err() { self.semantic_runtime_state = original } restore — leaving self.semantic_runtime_state EMPTY and silently destroying every fact emitted by prior COMMITTED sibling rules. SEMTRACE proof: RESTORE fired 0× / took post-body state (self.state→EMPTY) 9×. FIX (engine, in the generator): wrap the fallible body in an immediately-invoked closure (“try-block” emulation) so every ? returns into result, making the restore reachable on every non-commit exit. Zero unsafe; zero behaviour change on success. (RAII Drop-guard considered for strict panic-safety; deferred — needs *mut+unsafe due to &self-method borrow conflicts; IIFE+Default-validity is already panic-robust.) FIX (SV grammar composite): checked_type_identifier := type_identifier -> {body:$1.body} + @predicate has_fact args:[type_name,$body] phase:post, routed known_unscoped_block/data_type_identifier through it (proven .3.3.1/.3.3.2 declared-id idiom). Release bump, NO schema bump — affected declarations were silently unparseable so no such AST was ever emitted; previously-PARSEABLE byte-identical; only previously-erroring now succeed (strictly-more-permissive, SVPP-0002/REGEX-0083 category). VERIFIED: minimal repro my_t [3:0] x PASSES (was unfixable); SEMTRACE confirmed RESTORE fires 110× (was 0); use-site has_fact[type_name,my_t] resolves+true; class/typedef/localparam/let/#(parameter…)/builtin-dim no-regression. Inventory 2297→2299 (+2: the new wrapper rule). SV shape-contract GREEN (samples=3 aligned=3 drift=0 regression_lock_failures=0). regex broader corpus / RGX conformance ✅ 44/0 (critical downstream unaffected — non-semantic grammars hit the fast-path). external-corpus stays 6/14 — .3.3.3 is the FOUNDATION engine fix (state-leak was masking everything); residual 8 cases blocked by DISTINCT defects → .3.3.4 (cross-package import pkg::* type-name visibility — the actual corpus mover for ~6 cases) + .3.3.6 (statement-level, friscv_rv32i ×2). Pre-existing auto_gate_regex/rtl_const_expr_inventory_wide_shape failures tracked as .3.3.5.

0.59.01.0.58SV-Slice-58 audit: horizontal {first, rest} → [$N, $M::2*] extraction-spread fix across 49 grammar locations. Not a typing slice — a horizontal correctness audit applied retroactively to typed annotations introduced across earlier slices. Replaces the {first: $N, rest: $M} pattern (which exposed raw [[sep, item], ...] envelope of (sep X)* Quantified-of-Sequence) with [$N, $M::2*] (clean flat array of items, separators dropped) for every Category A rule (pure X (sep X)* with single payload per iteration). The annotation language has a first-class extraction-spread operator $N::M* defined in grammars/return_annotation.ebnf lines 50-58 and self-applied at line 158. Affected rules: assignment_pattern, attribute_instance, bind_target_instance_list, case_generate_item, case_item, class_constructor_arg_list_sv_2023, concatenation, cond_predicate, constant_concatenation, data_type enum branch, dist_list, let_port_list, list_of_arguments_{mixed,ordered,named}, list_of_checker_port_connections, list_of_clocking_decl_assign, list_of_cross_items, list_of_defparam_assignments, list_of_genvar_identifiers, list_of_net_assignments, list_of_net_decl_assignments, list_of_param_assignments, list_of_parameter_assignments_sv_2017, list_of_parameter_value_assignments_sv_2023, list_of_path_inputs/outputs, list_of_port_connections, list_of_ports, list_of_specparam_assignments, list_of_type_assignments, list_of_udp_port_identifiers, list_of_variable_assignments, list_of_variable_decl_assignments, net_lvalue concat-branch, open_range_list_sv_2017, package_export_declaration explicit-branch, package_import_declaration, pattern_sv_2017/2023 ordered-branch, production_sv_2017, range_list_sv_2023, rs_case_item_sv_2017/2023, rs_production_sv_2023, tf_port_list, udp_declaration_port_list, udp_port_list, variable_lvalue concat-branch, wait_order_statement events.
